body: However, compared to the picture quality of an OLED like the Samsung S95H, the Bravia 9 II's deep blacks looked less realistic. That's because on OLED TVs, the LEDs can be turned off entirely. The Bravia 9 II performed OK for Toy Story 5, but in darker scenes late in the film, I noticed the Samsung had inky blacks that reminded me of a high-end projector.My main takeaway is that it's nice that you can tweak settings on the Bravia 9 II to great effect, thanks to an RGB panel that’s super-bright. The movies Awake and The Creator tested my patience a little in that regard. I adjusted the black level to precisely 61 (out of 100) and could then see faces, a predawn mountain scene, and a beach landing with better clarity. Knowing you can achieve those results is nice; actually doing it does take time.Games and Everything ElseWhile playing Resident Evil: Requiem to test brightness, picture quality, and latency, I confirmed that it's possible to adjust the black level to liven up dark scenes. I also noticed that the latency, at a 120-Hz refresh rate when I used one of the HDMI 2.1 ports, was almost nonexistent. That helped with every slight twitch when a seven-headed monster from the dark underworld of hell started attacking me.Similar games, like Senua's Saga: Hellblade II, looked too gray and washed out on the midrange Bravia 7 II and some LED models I’ve tested. I also played End of Abyss, a game that takes place almost entirely in dark hallways, and the Bravia 9 II rendered those scenes with inky blacks—granted, not as black as an OLED would, but better than many LED TVs.Photograph: John BrandonBravia 9 II lived up to its flagship-quality promise for sportscasts, making my beloved Minnesota Vikings' purple jerseys look vivid and clear and the grass bright green—all without displaying any glare at all. News programs were bright, with strong color accuracy, but not oversaturated—a good compromise. In fact, it was so clear, I felt as if I could reach out to clip an MS Now analyst's nose hairs.Should You Buy It?The Bravia 9 II is near the top of the leaderboard of the best televisions to buy right now. You'll just want to consider the technology it uses. RGB models use red, green, and blue LEDs to create realistic colors that, in theory, improve color accuracy and vividness. Unlike an OLED TV, an RGB TV still shines those LED colors through an LCD panel. So you have to pick your poison. The Bravia 9 II looked super bright and vivid, especially during NFL games. It’s just a hair less colorful and vivid compared to the LG Micro RGB Evo.Knowing you can tweak the settings for the results you want and that anyone in your household will be able to see America’s Got Talent from any angle in the room is a major plus. But is the Sony Bravia 9 II worth $3,600 when so many TVs cost around $2,000? I would say it depends on what you watch. I want to see dragons at night and monsters in dark hallways, but for some animated shows, sports, and network TV, you might just want your device to work well, right out of the box, without worrying about cinematic quality. Yes, a flagship lets you do a lot more, but at a much steeper price.Power up with unlimited access to WIRED. description: Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing fi
body: Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.If you use Google’s apps and AI, it’s worth looking at this all-inclusive service. We break down the plans and how much they cost.Save up to 14% Off These Google Workspace Promo Codes 2026There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.Google is making changes to its productivity suite again, and some of it may cost you money. Here's what you need to know.What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.AI can tackle your email mountain so you don't have to. Here's how to decide whether Gmail's new productivity feature makes sense for your workflow.Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.Learn how to use keyboard shortcuts instead of mouse clicks for common tasks in Google Docs. You might be surprised at how much time you save.Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google WorkspaceGoogle has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.Adjust your options for things like account recovery, ad personalization, and which parts of your Google profile are shared publicly.

title: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘GTA VI’ Slop
description: Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Depar
body: Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”Another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.Among police departments that were not seeking to add to their ranks through GTA VI fever, many posted content aimed at reminding people that laws exist in real life. “Keep It In The Game VI,” advised a typical post on the Instagram account of the Glendale Police Department in California, complete with a GTA-fied police cruiser and view of the city. “Follow posted speed limits, respect the law, and keep your wanted level at ZERO!” the caption warned. The Denver Police Department, in similarly scolding fashion, informed followers: “Grand theft auto is still illegal.”The communications teams for these agencies should have perhaps reconsidered trying to farm engagement and clout from the massive success of GTA VI. As many commenters are noting, the game portrays cops as corrupt and quick to violence. Players have discovered that the Vice City squad will brutalize you if you start filming them during a questionable arrest. One clip showed a cop pulling his weapon on a character who had done nothing worse than stand in the street to take a selfie.A certain dose of this authoritarian cruelty ought to appeal to the right-wing cranks upset that GTA VI is too “woke” when it comes to gender, race, and politics overall. It’s a little different when the most visible villains of the game are choosing to overlook its vicious take on their profession in order to spam epic social media posts.Fox News, just for comparison, dutifully took the tired law-and-order line on GTA VI, with talking heads aghast at kids’ exposure to virtual gun violence (never mind actual gun deaths in the US) and an atmosphere of moral depravity. Elon Musk famously declared that he couldn’t play GTA games because they compelled you to shoot cops.Both stances, however insincere, suggest a modicum of regard for law enforcement that the police departments themselves immediately jettisoned in favor of GTA cringe. They of course won’t win any cool points for it, but at least this way they can pretend to connect with the general population.More baffling still is that the Russian army has generated its own GTA VI recruitment ads to blast out on its Telegram channel, and NATO has trumpeted its defensive security alliance with military-industrial GTA sludge, boasting that “even the best gamers would have a challenge” eluding fighter jets and submarines. Trying to parse Vice President JD Vance’s depiction of a Trumpian “golden age” with GTA graphics is a fool’s errand. In the most dystopian development of all, a US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the new GTA in return for reenlisting for another two years of service.What do any of these institutions or their missions have to do with a video game where you rob convenience stores in flip-flops? Doesn’t matter. When the zeitgeist is this all-consuming, you fire up ChatGPT and find an angle, no matter how confusing. Surely someone, somewhere, will be tricked into thinking you have anything to do with it.

title: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
description: When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says,
body: When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.”The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.“Even if you're not a CEO or at a big tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.“Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One company is pitching its new line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), says that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”Fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy.The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says.To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she says, is “a mind fuck.”Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection company Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.When tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”That setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he says. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.Catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.On Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI launched a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where users can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.It made sense, she says, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin says, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.)High-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, says Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the company and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler says.It’s particularly difficult, says Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.“Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey says. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”

title: Don’t Bring Jensen Back
description: Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three t
body: Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?)There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.This is an edition of Steven Levy and Lauren Goode’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

title: The Smart Ring Goes to Church
description: Stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing
body:
Stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.The first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps. Two new devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of users, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.Hallowed Be Thy NameBoth are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring launched in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech company ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.Another big player in prayer apps is Hallow, aimed at Catholics, backed by Vice President JD Vance’s Narya venture capital firm and celebrity ambassadors, with 24 million installs to date. Hallow’s toe-dip into wearables was a 2024 smart rosary with NFC embedded in the crucifix, made with Italian brand Ghirelli; Everblessed tried an earbud, necklace, and bedside device before settling on the ring design.Everblessed's Elah Ring S1.
Courtesy of Everblessed TechnologyHead-to-head on design, the Elah and Glorify rings are both made from titanium alloy, with a thorn-inspired twist for Glorify and a minimalist band featuring a cross for the Elah S1, which is also IP68 waterproof to 5 meters.For now, the Elah Ring is slightly techier: prayer reminders come via the cross, which glows via an LED, and “gentle” vibrations; these can pulse at certain times of day or be triggered by changes in heart rate and stress levels, picked up by a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor. Glorify’s CEO Henry Costa tells WIRED these emotion-based reminders will land on the Glorify Ring in six months; for now, you can set the times of day you want prayer reminders, track heart rate, blood oxygen, stress, and sleep via the optical sensor.One addition to the Glorify Ring that Costa says he personally uses “a lot” is recording prayers straight into the built-in mic. The ring has a light to signal when it's recording, and the app transcribes them. Everblessed CEO Ricky Xia says that, after consulting with pastors and users, the feeling was that voice notes on the ring were seen as “suspicious.” It’s available in-app, but most people don’t pray out loud, and too many features drain the battery life. (The Elah Ring runs for up to six days on one charge; Glorify for four to five days.)Both companies see the smart ring nudges helping wearers prioritize meaningful quiet time, away from screens, while offering in-app Christian practices as an alternative to Eastern meditation. Glorify offers Bible study, courses, and meditations. Blessed has devotional “anchors,” Bible texts and audio, plus guided breathing. Xia says he’s happy if the Elah vibrates and a user picks up a paper Bible rather than the Blessed app, while Costa says he’s “crying out to use my phone less.”The AI PastorThe Glorify Ring.
Courtesy of GlorifyBoth Glorify (founded in 2020, now merged with ConfideIn and headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area) and Blessed (founded in 2023 and based in San Jose) operate in more than 150 countries. Perhaps the biggest difference between the two rings is their relationship to AI.Xia is all-in, describing the S1 as an “AI-native” product, with a pastor-complementing, not-replacing FaithMate chatbot in the Blessed app, customized based on preferences, congregation, and depth of learning. ChatGPT is like a “good coworker,” he says, while FaithMate is designed to be “your friend” and an agent that can also handle secular tasks.“A lot of our users not only ask questions about the Bible but also ask about themselves, their relationships with their wives, they’re being bullied at school," Xia says, stressing safeguards around data storage, encryption, and privacy. "Everyone is going to have some AI that they trust, and how they view that is built on their personal stuff, their private vulnerabilities.”Costa is more circumspect, treading carefully on the consumer-facing side and noting that the Pope has weighed in with a 6,000-word encyclical on AI. A launch interview with CBN News garnered negative comments: “AI is Antichrist Information,” for one.“The stance I’ve always taken is that our daily devotional is hand-authored by a team of theologians,” Costa says. “It’s prayed over, and that is a stamp of approval.” He criticizes AI slop prayer apps as inauthentic. Still, he says the Glorify team has already tested “many forms” of AI personalization: “Any time, if we do use AI, it must be very clear to the user.”Spiritual HackingSmart ring owners were finding ways to add faith features to mainstream accessories before these rings came to fruition. For 20 years, timer and reminder apps have helped with prayer schedules, but recent examples are more creative. Heidi Campbell, professor of communication in religious studies at Texas A&M, refers to these DIY upgrades to the Oura ring and devices like the Muse headband as “spiritual mind-body hacking.”Everblessed's Elah Ring S1.
Courtesy of Everblessed TechnologyOura owners on #christiantiktok chat about how they already use the ring’s stress and HR alerts as a prompt to pause and reflect, as per Elah.Smart ring users flag changes in resting heart rate and sleep quality with scripture following their daily practice. “It’s really helpful for, like, what was inhibiting me from getting to a meditative or contemplative prayer state?” Campbell says. “It takes some of the mystery out of prayer, I think, but that can also be positive. There is a way to do prayer well and not well.” Ring hackers can also dig into health stats during Lent, Ramadan, and Yom Kippur to analyze energy expenditure and how fasting periods affect their bodies.The connected Christian ring is likely to remain niche, but that doesn’t mean the products will flop. James Stables, head of communications at smart ring manufacturer Ultrahuman, notes that attaching Christian practices to a trending category feels like a smart play. “Like prayer beads, the ring is analog in its on-body form and kind of tactile and haptic," he says.AI-powered voice recordings and emerging attempts at emotion tracking are part of a new phase for smart rings, says Ekta Mittal, a senior analyst of connected devices at CCS Insight. These new “purpose-driven” features extend wearable tech into “new parts of consumers’ daily routines,” Mittal says. She suggests that while Glorify and Everblessed will add value for some, the rings are “not directly competing” with established smart ring giants like Oura, Ultrahuman, and Samsung.The pandemic sped up the digital transition of many places of worship when congregations could not meet up in person, encouraging experimentation with social media. So it’s early days for Silicon Valley’s impact on organized religion. Researchers at the University of Würzburg in Germany, led by Ilona Nord, are studying the theological implications of using tech, including smart rings, for spiritual practices, investigating which values are baked into secular devices and apps.Campbell suggests many Christian groups haven’t stopped to consider the unintentional consequences of cultivating spirituality via personal tech. “All of these things are about individualizing the practice, which is good, but the challenges are for religions which are really focused on communal aspects,” she says. Not everyone has the money or connectivity to access these gadgets, but also, more existentially, “it puts spiritual development over communal development.”Xia points to the Blessed app’s communities, including its Healing Room broadcast feature, which lets pastors go live with sermons. It's not in the Elah app yet, but it's on the roadmap. Costa says communal practice is a core pillar, highlighting the “social layer” of public notes made on Christian texts in-app and an upcoming Glorify Ring feature which will allow a user to pair their device with a family member’s ring: “When your loved one is feeling down, you’ll get a buzz to check in with them.”

body: What if I told you Brooks Running started out making ballet slippers and bathing shoes? Founded in 1914, the Seattle-based company spent decades making just about everything except running shoes, moving from baseball cleats to roller skates, football cleats, children’s shoes, and softball cleats. It wasn’t until 1972 that Brooks made running its focus, and the company has been refining the category ever since.Brooks introduced one of the industry’s earliest uses of EVA foam, developed the first running shoe with a breathable GORE-TEX upper, and introduced the Kinetic Wedge, an innovative design tailored to women’s anatomy.So, while Brooks may not be the trendiest brand, it has built a reputation for dependable support, comfort, and durability. Here at WIRED, Brooks has plenty of fans, especially for trail and gravel running. The company also offers apparel we regularly recommend, including sports bras, outerwear, and running bottoms.Brooks Running shoes are reasonably priced for performance running footwear, with many models hovering around $150. If you’re in the market for a new pair, I’ve rounded up the best Brooks Running promo codes and coupons worth checking out.Brooks Running Black Friday DealsIf you want new kicks for the new year, be sure to shop the Brooks Running Black Friday Deals & Cyber Monday Deals section, where you’ll find steep discounts on men’s and women’s running shoes, gear, and apparel. You’ll find deep discounts on popular shoe styles like the Adrenaline GTS 25 and the Glycerin Flex. Plus, when you shop the Brooks Running Black Friday sale, you’ll get a free gift with a $160 purchase.Score 20% Off Your First Order With Brooks Promo CodeIf you’ve never ordered from Brooks’ website before, new customers get 20% off their first order after subscribing to the email list. You can apply the one-time Brooks coupon code to top-selling shoes, like the Caldera 7 and Adrenaline shoes, as well as other gear and apparel. It’s an easy way to save on some of their top products and take your road and trail running game to the next level.More Brooks Coupons and OffersAre you already a member of Brooks Run Club? If you sign up, you get member perks like early access to sales, free standard shipping with no order minimum, and free express shipping on orders from Brooks. Membership also includes more runner-specific perks, such as a free birthday gift and the chance to earn prizes by syncing your fitness tracker and contributing research to the Brooks team. You can also win a chance to visit the Seattle flagship store and have your gait analyzed by Brooks’ team. To join, visit Brooks Run Club and register using the Brooks promo code.If you shop and buy a complete outfit in one transaction from one of Brooks’ recommended buying guides—like Warm Weather Running Outfits or Fall Weather Running Outfits—you can get 15% off automatically applied at checkout. This is a fantastic deal if you only just realized in the past 10 days that you’ve been running in hail in your tiny shorts and cropped sports bra.Lightweight shoes now dominate the trails, so do you still need boots? Here’s how to choose the right footwear for your outdoor adventures.Save on Our Favorite Brooks Running ShoesBrooks makes so many iconic running shoes that it’s hard to list them all. I’m currently running in the Brooks Glycerin Max, which is one of the cushiest shoes I’ve ever tried. I don’t feel particularly stable on uneven terrain, but the padding is noticeably springy and cushy if you’ve been putting in some serious miles. WIRED director Michael Calore is a fan of the Brooks Ghost line, and if you’re planning to hit the trails in the cold, wet Pacific Northwest, I’d suggest the Brooks Cascadia Gore-Tex. The Adrenaline is the company’s most popular shoe.Photograph: Kieran AlgerBrooksGlycerin MaxPreorder Your Favorite Glycerin NowOne of the most anticipated Brooks drops is the Glycerin line. These shoes are built to be durable while allowing freedom of movement and flexibility. The cushioned shoes are comfortable for running and movement on many types of terrain. Many shoes in the Glycerin line are available to pre-order, including the Glycerin Flex, Glycerin 23, and Glycerin GTS 23. Be sure to check out the Glycerin line to see which is best for you.The Cascadia Elite Is Available NowBrooks is constantly dropping new shoe styles, ensuring there’s a shoe for every runner. The new Cascadia Elite Brooks Running shoe is unisex and great for trail running, with PEBA cushioning, a Vibram Megagrip Elite outsole, and a MATRYX engineered woven upper with Kevlar fibers to help secure your feet firmly, no matter what terrain you’re traversing. This shoe has light, springy cushioning that helps propel you forward, whether that’s competitive trail racing, Sub-ultras, VKs, or ultras.Upcoming Brooks Sale Events to Watch Out ForDo you have a runner in your life? The odds are they’re taking stock of their winter apparel and shoes, deciding whether these leggings will make it through another winter. The best time to save is during seasonal sales, with discounts on footwear and apparel, including popular items like the Ghost 16 running shoes.Do you have running military, nurses, or first responders in your life? Brooks Running also offers 25% off full-priced items for verified community heroes with a Brooks promo code. Sign up here.Brooks Discount: Shop Pre-Owned Shoes at BrooksIf you’re looking for a new pair of shoes but don’t have the cash to invest in a brand-new, high-end pair, look no further than Brooks’ restock page, where gently used Brooks shoes are on sale at deeply discounted prices. They have both men’s and women’s sections, recently added shoes, and a breakdown of bestselling styles, including the Adrenaline, Ghost, Glycerin, and Hyperion.Brooks Coupon: 20% Off Join the Brooks Run ClubIf you’re looking to shop at Brooks, it’s a great idea to join the Brooks Run Club for additional perks and discounts. Some of the best benefits Run Club offers include a 20% discount on apparel when you join and an annual birthday gift. You’ll just need to log in or join the club to get the discount code.Brooks Sports Medicine Ambassador Program: 40% OffIf you’re a sports medicine professional, you can save big and get rewarded at Brooks Running. The Brooks Sports Medicine Ambassador Program is a free membership for eligible sports medicine professionals, a way to say thank you for the care they provide to runners and athletes. All you have to do is verify your status by signing in or creating an ID.me account to confirm your qualifications. Then, you’ll get a steep 40% discount on the first $1,000 spent on eligible items in Brooks Running online orders (it resets every January 1).Brooks Return Policy and 90 Day Wear TestBrooks knows how important gear is to athletes. So, you can take your Brooks gear for a 90-day trial run, and if you aren't satisfied, return it for free. If you’re at all unsatisfied with your Brooks purchase, you can return it for free with no shipping or restocking fees.

title: Pura’s Cyber Week Sale Is the Time to Stock Up on Scents
description: Over the past few years, WIRED has tested nearly every major brand of essential oil diffuser. Pura’s been our top nebulizer-style device (these work b
body: Over the past few years, WIRED has tested nearly every major brand of essential oil diffuser. Pura’s been our top nebulizer-style device (these work by blowing air through oil) for years due to its ease of use and sprawling library of high-end scents.In fact, no brand even comes close to Pura's sheer breadth of available fragrances—with more than 150 options from big names like Anthropologie, Nest, LAFCO, Brooklyn Candle Company, Studio McGee, and more. Pura even has special seasonal collabs, like this month’s Nutcracker-inspired scents from the New York City Ballet. These diffusers are also highly convenient to use in that you can control them from your phone via an app (the Home, Plus, and Car also have buttons on the actual devices).But, it's a luxury you'll pay for. If you own a Pura or have seen it in stores, you already know the scents aren't cheap; single cartridges range from $14 for Pura’s house line all the way up to $21 for name brands like Thymes and Votivo. (The prices displayed on Pura's website look lower, but that's only if you buy a recurring subscription—make sure you note the one-time purchase price.)Photograph: Kat MerckCartridges can last for a month or more in the Pura Mini, but in a larger diffuser like the Pura Plus, they may only last a couple of weeks. That's why the best time to stock up on scents for the year is during a sale, like Pura’s Cyber Week event. Right now through December 6, all fragrances are 20 percent off, and all diffusers are 30 percent off.Worth the BuyPura's diffuser lineup isn't perfect, but neither are any of the diffusers we've tried from any brand. Diffusers can be loud or messy, take up a lot of space, or have an uninspiring line of scents. Pura's Mini and Car models are worthwhile yet quirky (though I can't recommend the Plus), but the Home has given me no issues in six months of testing.Pura HomePhotograph: Louryn StrampePhotograph: Louryn StrampeCourtesy of PuraPuraHome Smart Home Fragrance DiffuserIf you're in the market for a Pura diffuser, our top pick for most people is the new Pura Home. The first Pura I ever owned was the 3 model, and I've also had the 4, but the 5 (rebranded “Home”) improves on just about everything, with dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi compatibility; faster diffusion; control buttons on the device itself; and even a new way to load cartridges, where you can slide out the bottom portion (which is flat to sit on a surface), seat the scents, and click it into place. QR codes on the cartridges inform your app which scents they are and when they were loaded, so it can, in turn, remind you when it's time to replace them. I also like that this model is totally silent.Pura MiniPhotograph: Kat MerckPuraMini Smart Home Fragrance DiffuserI also recommend the oval-shaped Mini—I have one in my office right now. Though you can only control it via Pura's app, scents last for over a month, and it does a great job at scenting a smaller space like a bedroom. My unit makes a high-pitched ringing noise, almost like an ultrasonic pest repellent, which is annoying, but Pura's customer service will likely replace yours if this happens to you.Pura CarPhotograph: Kat MerckPuraCar Smart Fragrance DiffuserThere’s also the Pura Car, whose refills I will be purchasing during this sale (MSRP averages $21 apiece, and the four-week run time has been roughly accurate in my experience). Online reviews of this device are mixed, but I love mine. If you’re a parent, having Pura scents to inhale instead of old, spilled food and stinky soccer cleats is 100 percent worth the spend. Buy one for a mom you know, but only if she has USB charging ports in her car—it needs to be plugged in most of the time, as it doesn’t hold a charge for very long.Pura Advent CalendarCourtesy of PuraPuraAdvent CalendarAlso on sale for 20 percent off is Pura's fun new Advent calendar, which features a Pura Home diffuser and 12 best-selling scents, most of which I have tried and can vouch for being options most people would enjoy.About the Pura PlusAnother Pura Cyber Week deal: Spend $50, and get 50 percent off the Pura Plus diffuser for large spaces, which has an MSRP of $80. I didn’t have the best of luck with the two Plus devices I went through—both eventually developed a loud buzzing noise. (Note that Pura will send you a replacement if this happens to you.) Additionally, unlike the Puras that sit flush to the outlet, this one is a cylinder that sits apart and must be plugged in at all times. It also makes an audible, fixed “shhhhhhh” noise as it’s long as it’s on (unlike the more intermittent noise emitted by competitors). However, it did do a great job of scenting a high-ceilinged room on the first floor of my house.Power up with unlimited access to WIRED. That’s why, instead of heels and dress shoes, you see everyone in NYC wearing some riff on comfortable sneakers. Brooks, Hoka, New Balance, and yes, Skechers.Skechers isn’t the flashiest brand, but its shoes prioritize comfort and reasonable prices across a slew of categories: running, walking, hiking, home, and work, to name a few. In the 90s, it aligned with utility boots and grunge fashion, but it quickly grew to focus on casual, comfortable, and athletic shoes for basically everyone. Today, you’ll see some of Skechers' most prominent shoe lines, including “Cozy Fit”, “Slip-ins”, and “Wide Fit”.Like most brands, it also offers a few Skechers coupons, promo codes, and online offers that can help you save a few bucks at checkout.
